summary:
Gibraltar is a self-governing British Overseas Territory with its own Parliament and its own Supreme Court, which between them make and interpret its civil and criminal law. Measures enacted by the United Kingdom do not apply here of their own force: the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex-services code issued in 2025 bind Gibraltar only if extended by Order in Council, and no such extension appears in the sourced material.

The principal legal gap facing a trans visitor is gender recognition. No process exists in Gibraltar for changing a legal gender marker, and the sourced material records that transgender persons are not permitted to change legal gender. A trans visitor therefore travels on a document whose marker cannot be altered by any local route, and can expect to be read at the border and in public under that marker.

Statutory discrimination protection covering gender reassignment has been in place since the Equal Opportunities Act 2006 took effect on 1 March 2007. The Act prohibits discrimination in employment and in the provision of goods and services on the ground of gender reassignment, defined as a process for the purpose of reassigning a person's sex by changing physiological or other attributes of sex. Sexual orientation is also a protected ground under the same Act.

Hate-crime coverage now extends to trans people. Parliament amended the Crimes Act in September 2013 to criminalise hatred and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, with royal assent on 25 September and effect from 10 October 2013. In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill amending hate crime and hate speech legislation to include protections for transgender identity.

In July 2026 Parliament also passed a bill making it an offence to offer or practise conversion therapy. The sourced excerpt states the offence generally without specifying whether its scope covers sexual orientation, transgender identity, or both.

Partner and family recognition is established locally: civil partnerships since March 2014, same-sex marriage since December 2016 after the Civil Marriage Amendment Act passed unanimously on 26 October 2016, received royal assent on 1 November and took effect on 15 December 2016, with the first marriage the following day. A deputy registrar may opt out, requiring assignment of an alternative registrar. The Supreme Court ruled on 10 April 2013 that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Gibraltar Constitution, and the Adoption Act 2023 took full effect on 18 April 2024, expressly allowing same-sex couples to adopt without discrimination.

The age of consent for all sexual activity regardless of sexuality or gender is 16. The Supreme Court ruled on 8 April 2011 that the previous age of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional, and the gender-neutral Crimes Act 2011, approved in August 2011, set the equal age of 16 with effect from 23 November 2012.

Reproductive and family formation routes are open to same-sex couples: in June 2017 the Gibraltar Health Authority amended its IVF policy to allow lesbian couples access to assisted reproductive technology, and in February 2021 Gibraltar enacted a surrogacy law permitting non-commercial, altruistic surrogacy for married couples or civil partners unable to conceive, with automatic recognition of children of same-sex couples conceived through artificial insemination.

The House of Commons Foreign Affairs Committee's 2008 inquiry into overseas territories recommended that discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender status be made illegal in all overseas territories, and its Seventh Report of 2007-08 sets accountability and good-governance expectations applicable to Gibraltar.
tangentialFactors:
The Ministry for Justice and Equality said on 22 July 2021 that it would 'urgently' consider legislation to tackle what it called 'disgusting lurking homophobia' following an incident of anti-gay abuse; in July 2021 the Justice Ministry was investigating a proposal to make denigration of a person on the basis of sexual orientation a specific criminal offence, prompted by Chief Minister Fabian Picardo's description of social-media abuse during Pride month. This indicates an official posture willing to legislate against identity-based abuse, though the sourced material records no comparable trans-specific incident.

The 2006 Constitution does not mention sexual orientation, after 2002 proposals to include it were omitted; protection rests on statute rather than constitutional text.

Male same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised in 1993 following pressure from the European Court of Human Rights and the United Kingdom Government, with no equivalent provision for women because the Victorian-drafted law only addressed men. A private member's bill to equalise the age of consent was defeated in Parliament on 18 May 2009 before the courts and the Crimes Act 2011 resolved the issue.

The December 2015 consultation on same-sex marriage left Gibraltarians polarised, according to El País (15 August 2016), though an inter-ministerial committee, popular consultation and the main parties suggested support for the change; the bill nonetheless passed Parliament unanimously in October 2016.

The Foreign Affairs Committee's Seventh Report (2007-08) also records corruption concerns raised in Turks and Caicos, a separate overseas territory, which is context for the committee's governance expectations rather than a Gibraltar finding.

Local residents therefore live under a fixed marker on Gibraltar-issued documentation with no domestic remedy.

Residents may marry or form civil partnerships regardless of gender, adopt under the Adoption Act 2023 as in full effect from 18 April 2024, and access altruistic surrogacy under the February 2021 law and IVF under the amended Gibraltar Health Authority policy of June 2017.

outOfScopeNotes:
The sourced material does not resolve whether the July 2026 conversion-therapy bill's scope covers gender identity, sexual orientation, or both; the excerpt states the offence generally.

Whether the July 2026 hate-crime and hate-speech amendments have entered into force, and their penalties, is not stated in the inventory; only the date of parliamentary passage is recorded.

No enforcement data, incident counts, or complaint outcomes under the Equal Opportunities Act's gender-reassignment ground appear in the inventory, so the practical reach of the 2007 protection is unverified here.

The inventory records no trans-specific violence incidents, arrests, or border incidents in Gibraltar; the July 2021 homophobia episode cited is anti-gay abuse, not documented as trans-directed.
